label: Chapter 8: From Steel to Finance, and Luxembourg Today, 1980 to 2026

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In the early nineteen-eighties, the steel industry that had built modern Luxembourg was shrinking.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Blast furnaces closed and thousands of jobs vanished.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In many European industrial regions, that kind of decline led to decades of misery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg took a different path, because a new industry was already growing in its shadow: banking and finance.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The seeds went back to the first Eurobond.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the following decades the Grand Duchy built itself into a major international financial center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Banks from around the world set up offices, attracted by its stability, its multilingual workforce, its flexible laws, and its famously strong banking secrecy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1988, Luxembourg was the first country to write a 1985 European directive on cross-border investment funds into national law, which gave it a head start in that business.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And today?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is the largest center for investment funds in Europe, second in the world only to the United States, and by common estimates the financial sector accounts for roughly a quarter of the whole economy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened to the steel company?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2002, ARBED merged with Spanish and French rivals to form Arcelor, which in 2006 was taken over by the steel group of the Indian-born businessman Lakshmi Mittal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The result was ArcelorMittal, one of the largest steelmakers in the world, still headquartered in Luxembourg City.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the old steel country found new uses for its industrial heritage.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At Belval, in the far south near Esch, one of the biggest steelworks was shut down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its enormous blast furnaces weren't demolished.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They were preserved as monuments, and around them rose a whole new district, with offices, a concert hall called the Rockhal, and the campus of the University of Luxembourg, which was founded only in 2003.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Where workers once tapped molten iron, students now study for exams.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In June 1985, on a passenger boat anchored on the Moselle near the Luxembourg village of Schengen, five European countries signed an agreement to gradually abolish border checks among them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Schengen is a tiny wine-growing village where the borders of Luxembourg, France and Germany meet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Schengen Area, which now lets millions of people cross borders without passport control, was born on that boat.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then the euro.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the early nineties, as leaders negotiated the Maastricht Treaty, which set the path to a single currency, Luxembourg's finance minister was a young politician named Jean-Claude Juncker.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A crafty, informal negotiator, he helped broker the compromises that made the deal possible.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He became prime minister in 1995 and held the job for eighteen years, longer than any other head of government in the European Union at the time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He later chaired the eurozone finance ministers through the debt crisis, and in 2014 he was chosen as President of the European Commission.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: He wasn't the first Luxembourger in that job.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Gaston Thorn led the Commission from 1981 to 1985, and Jacques Santer from 1995 to 1999.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Three presidents from one of the smallest countries in the union is an extraordinary record.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It reflects what Luxembourg has always been good at: making deals among bigger partners, and making itself indispensable.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What about the language?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1984, Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect spoken at home for centuries, was formally recognized as the national language.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: French and German remained the languages of law and administration.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Children grow up with three languages in school, and many speak English, Portuguese or Italian at home as well.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In few countries is multilingualism such a normal part of daily life.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the country grew rich and crowded.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg has about two thirds of a million residents, and nearly half hold a foreign passport.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On top of that, around two hundred thousand people cross the border every day from France, Belgium and Germany to work.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Per head, it has one of the highest standards of living in the world, but also some of the highest housing costs in Europe, and legendary traffic jams on the roads into the capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2020, the government made all public transport free for everyone, the first country in the world to do so.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it looked to the sky.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A Luxembourg-based company, SES, launched the Astra satellites in the nineteen-eighties, one of Europe's great satellite television success stories.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2017, the government passed a law on space resources, and in 2018 it created its own space agency, hoping to become a hub for the new space economy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not everything has been smooth.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2008, Grand Duke Henri, who had come to the throne in 2000 when his father Jean abdicated, announced that his conscience would not allow him to sign a bill legalizing euthanasia.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The government responded by changing the constitution, so that the Grand Duke simply promulgates laws rather than approving them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A quiet change that further reduced the monarch's role.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And LuxLeaks.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2014, a leak of confidential documents revealed that Luxembourg had signed tax deals with hundreds of multinational companies, allowing them to pay very low taxes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The outcry across Europe was fierce, and many officials elsewhere said the Grand Duchy had been undermining its neighbors.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The government defended its legal framework but came under heavy pressure, and in 2015 it joined an international system for the automatic exchange of bank account information, effectively ending the era of strict banking secrecy for foreign account holders.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The debate over what is fair in international taxation continues.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the politics?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Christian Social party dominated for most of the twentieth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From 2013 to 2023, a three-party coalition of liberals, Greens and social democrats governed under Prime Minister Xavier Bettel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the election of October 2023, the Greens lost heavily and the coalition lost its majority.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A new government took office in November 2023, led by Luc Frieden of the Christian Social party, in coalition with Bettel's Democratic Party.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Frieden is prime minister, and Bettel is deputy prime minister and foreign minister.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And one more big moment, the most recent chapter of the oldest story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-third of June, 2025, Luxembourg's National Day, Grand Duke Henri announced that he would step down after twenty-five years on the throne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the third of October, 2025, in a ceremony at the Grand Ducal Palace, he formally abdicated in favor of his eldest son, Guillaume.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was forty-three.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He swore an oath to the constitution before parliament, and greeted crowds from a balcony of the palace with his Belgian-born wife, Stéphanie, and their two young sons beside him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He is the seventh grand duke of the modern line that began with Adolphe in 1890.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Voluntary abdication has become something of a tradition in this family, since Henri himself took the throne when his father stepped aside in 2000.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So let's step back and look at the whole journey.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It began in nine sixty-three with a count and a rock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It passed through a golden age of emperors who sat on the thrones of Prague, Budapest and Rome.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a fortress that foreign armies fought over for centuries, passed from Burgundy to Spain to France to Austria and back to France again.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then it was created as a grand duchy in 1815.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Carved in half in 1839, saved from a war in 1867, occupied by Germany twice, and each time it recovered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It turned from farms into steel, from steel into finance, and from a nation guarding itself into one of the founding pillars of a united Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And through all of it, one thing stayed consistent.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The people of this small land, who have spoken three languages and lived under a dozen flags, never stopped insisting on being themselves.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The line from that old song, written in the eighteen-fifties, still works as a national motto: Mir wëlle bleiwe wat mir sinn.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: We want to remain what we are.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That is the story of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Thank you for listening, and safe travels.
